explanations: luna: The source section traces ش ر ح through cutting and spreading, then says a gathered thing opens and its interior is revealed. In this ayah, after hardened hearts are compared to stone, some rocks split and water comes out; it gives a concrete nonlexical parallel of a hard, closed body opening to release what is within.

terra: The question about telling believers what God had opened to the speakers can carry the sense of disclosing revealed knowledge; if that reading is intended, it tentatively parallels the section's speech sense of making hidden meaning visible.
terra: The claim “our hearts are wrapped” and the answer that disbelief has brought a curse present inward enclosure as the refusal opposed to an expanded breast.
terra: وَمَن يَرْغَبُ عَن مِّلَّةِ إِبْرَٰهِيمَ uses رغبة with عَنْ for turning away, a grammatical and moral reversal of directing it with إِلَى toward the Lord.
terra: God explicitly intends ease for people and does not intend hardship, stating as a divine purpose the same ease-versus-difficulty relation that follows the section's opened breast.

terra: On the traditional reading in which Abraham is told to cut the birds, their portions are distributed over the hills; this only tentatively recalls the source dictionary's cutting-and-spreading of flesh because the command's exact action is interpreted in more than one way.
terra: The prayer asks God not to lay a burden on people or make them carry what exceeds their capacity; it makes explicit why opening space and putting down a load belong together in the section.

luna: The source section's dictionary sense of ش ر ح is opening difficult speech to reveal hidden meanings. This ayah distinguishes “مُتَشَابِهَاتٌ” from clear verses and warns against seeking their interpretation “ٱبْتِغَاءَ ٱلْفِتْنَةِ”; it bounds the work of opening obscurity with the risk of manufacturing discord.

luna: The source section names root ص د ر for the bodily chest and describes opening as bringing an interior into view. This ayah speaks of what people “فِي صُدُورِكُمْ,” whether concealed or disclosed before Allah, making the chest's inside-and-outside boundary explicit. | terra: Whether people conceal what is in their breasts or disclose it, God knows it; the concealment/disclosure pair corresponds to the section's account of an interior becoming visible when opened.
terra: Hatred has appeared from people's mouths while what their breasts hide is greater, joining outward speech to a still-folded inward content in the precise relation the section distinguishes.

luna: The source section names root ص د ر for the bodily chest. This ayah describes people whose breasts are “حَصِرَتْ” at the prospect of fighting you or their own people; that specific constriction counters the opened chest with a scene of fear and withdrawal. | terra: حَصِرَتْ صُدُورُهُمْ presents breasts too constricted to fight either their own people or the believers, a concrete opposite to a breast made spacious for its charge.

terra: The verse uses the رغبة verb concerning marrying orphan women without an expressed directional preposition; because the construction has been read as desire for or aversion from marriage, it cautiously illustrates why the root's direction must be specified.
terra: After prescribing purification, God says He does not wish to place constriction upon believers but to purify them and complete His favor, tying absence of حَرَج to an enabling benefaction.

luna: The source section's dictionary note treats the root و ز ر in 94:2 as a bundle packed in a spread garment. This ayah pictures people carrying “أَوْزَارَهُمْ عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِمْ,” giving the load a visible weight on the back that complements the section's bundled burden. | terra: Those who deny the meeting with God carry their burdens on their backs, giving the section's dictionary bundle-load a visible bodily form and clarifying the relief of removing such a load.

terra: God opens for heedless people the gates of everything until they exult, then seizes them suddenly; the harmful opening sharply supports the section's claim that openness alone does not determine its value.

luna: The source section's dictionary sense of ش ر ح is opening difficult speech to reveal what is hidden in it. This ayah calls the revealed Book “مُفَصَّلًا” while asking whether any judge but God should be sought, presenting the Book as laid out in detail for judgment.

luna: The source section names root ش ر ح for opening the chest. This ayah says God opens a breast for Islam, then sets a boundary with a chest made “ضَيِّقًا حَرَجًا,” likened to climbing into heaven; the paired outcomes show both capacity and constriction, while the opening's direction is guidance. | terra: God opens a person's breast to Islam, while the same ayah makes the breast constricted like someone laboriously ascending the sky; it states both the section's receptive expansion and its breathless opposite.

luna: The source section labels root و ز ر for the burden and gives it the image of a packed load. This ayah states “وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَىٰ,” setting individual accountability as a boundary beside the burden lifted for the addressee in surah 94. | terra: In the setting of each soul's own earning, no bearer bears another's burden; the rule marks the exceptional mercy in the section's address, where God Himself puts the addressee's load down.

luna: The source section names root ص د ر for the bodily chest. This ayah says “فَلَا يَكُن فِي صَدْرِكَ حَرَجٌ مِّنْهُ” about the revealed Book; the command against chest-distress sets a boundary beside the image of the chest opened for its recipient. | terra: The revealed Book comes with the command that there be no constriction in the Prophet's breast from it, so that he may warn; this directly links an unconfined breast with carrying speech to others.

luna: The source section names root ص د ر and describes opening as creating room within. This ayah says rancor is removed from the people of Paradise's breasts as they acknowledge that God guided them; the emptied interior makes room for reconciled fellowship. | terra: God removes the rancor within the inhabitants' breasts, showing relief as an actual extraction of harmful inward content from the bodily container the section opens.

luna: The source section's dictionary sense of ش ر ح is opening difficult speech so its meanings appear. This ayah says the people were given a Book detailed with knowledge, then identifies it as guidance and mercy for believers; the detail serves understanding and acceptance.

luna: The source section notes 94:2's burden as a bundle formed by spreading a garment and putting things inside. This ayah describes the Messenger removing “إِصْرَهُمْ” and the shackles from people; the parallel release from a carried load makes the surah's burden detail concrete. | terra: God's messenger “puts down from them their burden” and their shackles; the construction يَضَعُ عَنْهُمْ إِصْرَهُمْ closely parallels the section's burden put down from the addressee and shows relief as release.

luna: The source section defines root ص د ر as the bodily chest and notes a person who suffers chest trouble. This ayah says God heals the breasts of a believing people in the battle setting; it gives a direct bodily-chest counterpart to the section's opening of a constricted space. | terra: God's action through the believers is said to heal the breasts of a believing people, directly staging the chest as the place where hurt is felt and relieved.
terra: The continuation of healed breasts says God removes the rage of their hearts, specifying the painful inward content whose removal constitutes that healing.
terra: At Hunayn the earth becomes narrow for the believers despite all its breadth, repeating the precise paradox that outward width can coexist with experienced constriction.

luna: The source section names root ر غ ب and says its lexical origin is breadth in a thing; 94:8 turns that desire toward the Lord. This ayah calls the speakers “إِلَى اللَّهِ رَاغِبُونَ,” giving a direct instance of that orientation toward God. | terra: إِنَّآ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ رَٰغِبُونَ repeats the section's closing orientation of desire toward God, with the same إِلَى that directs the spacious impulse rather than leaving it aimless.
terra: For the three who stayed behind, the earth becomes narrow despite its breadth and their own selves become constricted; spacious surroundings cannot substitute for inward room.
terra: Believers near Medina are forbidden to prefer their own selves over the Messenger or hold themselves back from him; رغب with عَنْ again sets self-preserving withdrawal against Godward desire.

luna: The source section names root ص د ر for the chest and says it is opened to receive truth; it also describes explanation as making hidden meaning visible. This ayah calls revelation a healing for what is in the breasts, alongside admonition and guidance, joining revealed speech to the inner chest. | terra: The revelation is called a healing for what is in the breasts as well as guidance and mercy, treating the breast as the bodily-inner site whose trouble can be relieved and made receptive.

luna: The source section's dictionary sense of ش ر ح is opening difficult speech to reveal hidden meanings. This ayah describes a Book whose verses are first made firm and then expounded; it gives a specific scriptural formulation of content being laid out for understanding.

luna: The source section describes opening and spreading as making an interior visible. This ayah says people “يَثْنُونَ صُدُورَهُمْ” to hide from God; folded breasts used for concealment reverse the section's image of an opened interior. | terra: People bend or fold their breasts to hide from God, yet He knows what they conceal and disclose; this reverses the section's act of unfolding something so that its interior becomes visible.

luna: The source section names root ص د ر for the bodily chest. In this ayah the Prophet's chest is “ضَائِقٌ بِهِ صَدْرُكَ” because of what is revealed and the opponents' demands; it presents the constricted counterpart under the pressure of revelation. | terra: The Prophet's breast is described as constricted by the possibility of hostile demands leading him to leave part of revelation, locating the section's opened space within the pressure of proclamation.

terra: When the messengers reach Lot, he is distressed and feels straitened in his capacity to protect them; the bodily idiom of too little room parallels the section's chest made fit for a hard mission.

luna: The source section's dictionary sense of ش ر ح treats opening speech as spreading it to reveal hidden meanings, and it names root ص د ر for the chest. This ayah pairs “أَسَرَّ الْقَوْلَ” with God's knowledge of “ذَاتِ الصُّدُورِ,” joining the two concealed interiors developed in the section.

luna: The source section describes the opened chest as a space whose interior is exposed and cleared. This ayah says rancor is removed from the residents' breasts before describing them as brothers facing one another; the cleared chest gives a specific counterpart to the section's opened interior. | terra: God removes rancor from people's breasts and sets them face to face as brothers, a repeated direct picture of inward space cleared of what had occupied it.

luna: The source section names root ص د ر for the bodily chest. Here the Prophet's chest “يَضِيقُ صَدْرُكَ ... بِمَا يَقُولُونَ”; pressure from people's words gives a direct narrowing counterpart to the remembered opening. | terra: God tells the same prophetic addressee that He knows his breast is constricted by what people say, giving the bodily pressure whose relief the section's completed opening recalls.

terra: The immediate answer to the Prophet's constricted breast is to glorify his Lord with praise and prostrate, so the pressure of people's words is redirected toward the Lord just as the section finally directs رغبة.
terra: After the command to answer chest-constriction with praise and prostration, continued worship carries that redirection toward the Lord through the remainder of life.

luna: The source section labels root و ز ر for the burden and explains its bundle image as something spread and filled. This ayah uses “أَوْزَارَهُمْ” for burdens borne at resurrection, including burdens from those they misled; it shows how the load can accrue through one's acts. | terra: Misleaders carry their own burdens in full and some burdens of those they mislead, an accumulation opposite to the section's load being put down from its bearer.
terra: The Reminder is sent to the Prophet so that he may make clear to people what was sent down to them, staging the communicative work the section identifies as opening speech.

luna: The source section labels ش ر ح as opening and spreading the chest. Here “شَرَحَ بِالْكُفْرِ صَدْرًا” turns that act toward disbelief, marking the boundary that opening by itself does not determine its direction. | terra: مَّن شَرَحَ بِٱلْكُفْرِ صَدْرًا turns the same opening toward unbelief; the forced speaker whose heart remains secure in faith supplies the ayah's own boundary and confirms that opening takes its value from what enters it.
terra: The people who opened their breasts to unbelief are said to have preferred the nearer life over the hereafter, showing the preference that directed their opening toward the wrong content.
terra: Those same people then have hearts, hearing, and sight sealed; this contextual sequel sharply shows that opening oneself to unbelief produces closure of the faculties of reception.

luna: The source section's dictionary sense of ش ر ح includes spreading difficult speech so its hidden meaning appears. This ayah says each person will meet a record-book “مَنشُورًا”; an opened text makes its previously unseen contents available to its reader. | terra: Each person meets a record مَنشُورًا on resurrection, an opened record whose exposed contents make the section's physical “spread and reveal” operation concrete.

luna: After the spread record in 17:13, this ayah tells the person “اقْرَأْ كِتَابَكَ.” Its own contribution is the reading of the exposed contents, completing the section's image of difficult words opened so their meaning can be seen.

luna: The source section labels root و ز ر for the burden and gives it the image of a packed load. This ayah says “وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَىٰ” before stating that warning comes before punishment; its rule of personal burden marks a boundary beside the burden lifted for the addressee in surah 94. | terra: The rule that no bearer carries another's burden follows individual guidance or error, clarifying that removal “from you” concerns a genuinely personal charge.

terra: The youths are promised that their Lord will spread His mercy for them and prepare facility in their affair, joining divine spreading, beneficiary-marking, and a task made manageable just as the section does.

terra: The record is set down and found to have omitted nothing small or great, making an opened document's formerly contained detail fully visible in the way the section describes unfolding and disclosure.
terra: The people found between the barriers can scarcely understand speech, a specific communicative closure against which the section's dictionary sense of opening difficult words becomes visible.

terra: Abraham's father asks whether he is turning away from his gods, using رَاغِبٌ ... عَنْ; the hostile object makes especially clear how the preposition directs the root's openness away rather than toward.
terra: God says He has made the revelation easy in the Prophet's tongue, joining the section's linked images of eased difficulty, an opened tongue, and speech made available to its hearers.
terra: God tells the Prophet that the Quran was not sent down to make him suffer, situating revealed speech as a charge for which divine aid and inward capacity are supplied.

luna: The source section places Musa's request in 20:25 after this commission. “إِنَّهُ طَغَىٰ” identifies Pharaoh's transgression, making the requested opening a capacity for the difficult encounter rather than a free-floating mood. | terra: The command to go to the transgressing Pharaoh supplies the dangerous task that makes Moses' following request for chest-room concrete rather than a general wish for calm.

luna: The source section labels root ش ر ح as opening and spreading. Musa's prayer, “ٱشْرَحْ لِي صَدْرِي,” uses that same act on the same bodily chest; “لِي” makes it a request for himself, beside 94:1's reminder of work done for its addressee. | terra: Moses' exact prayer رَبِّ ٱشْرَحْ لِى صَدْرِى uses the section's ش ر ح image and reverses its stance: he asks “for me,” whereas the section recalls what God has already done “for you.”

luna: Immediately after Musa asks for his chest to be opened, he asks “وَيَسِّرْ لِي أَمْرِي.” The source section pairs this with ease after the remembered opening in surah 94; this line states what that requested capacity is to make easy: the task. | terra: Immediately after asking for his breast to be opened, Moses asks God to ease his task; this is the exact prayer-side sequence behind the section's movement from opening to ease.

luna: Musa asks “وَٱحْلُلْ عُقْدَةً مِّن لِّسَانِي.” The source section's dictionary sense of ش ر ح is to open difficult speech and reveal hidden meaning; Musa's request to loosen a tongue-knot makes the chest-to-speech connection explicit. | terra: Moses asks for a knot to be loosed from his tongue, making bodily the section's dictionary picture of difficult, knotted speech being opened.
terra: “That they may understand my speech” states the purpose of loosening the tongue-knot, corresponding to the section's dictionary sense of opening difficult speech so its meaning can be seen.
terra: Still within the same prayer, Moses asks for a وَزِيرًا from his family; the helper sought to bear the mission's weight extends the section's load-and-capacity relation.
terra: Within the chest-opening prayer Moses asks God to strengthen his back through Aaron, linking expanded capacity to support at the very bodily place on which the section's load bears.
terra: Moses asks that Aaron share in his task, turning the relief sought by chest-opening into distributed responsibility rather than mere inward comfort.
terra: Moses says the requested chest-room, ease, and help will let them glorify God much, giving a Godward purpose to the capacity requested in the preceding prayer.
terra: Remembering God much is the second stated purpose of Moses' requested enabling, anticipating the section's movement from expanded capacity toward the Lord.

luna: After Musa's requests in 20:25–27, God replies “قَدْ أُوتِيتَ سُؤْلَكَ”; the section itself notes that Musa's wish was granted. This completes the contrast between Musa's petition and 94:1's reminder of work already done for its addressee. | terra: God's answer that Moses has been granted his request converts the preceding plea for chest-opening and ease into an accomplished gift, matching the section's shift from “for me” to “for you.”
terra: Moses' people say they were made to carry loads of the people's ornaments, a concrete carried cargo that preserves the bundle sense used to explain وِزْر.

luna: The source section labels root و ز ر for 94:2's burden and explains its dictionary image as a bundle formed by spreading and filling a garment. This ayah says one who turns away from the reminder will carry a burden on the Day of Resurrection, a concrete use of that load-image. | terra: Whoever turns away from the Reminder will carry a وِزْر on resurrection, placing the same named burden upon a person instead of taking it away.

luna: Following the burden in 20:100, this ayah calls it an evil load on the Day of Resurrection. The source section's dictionary gloss treats 94:2's burden as a packed bundle; this continuation gives the weight-bearing result its own force. | terra: The following ayah calls that burden an evil load on resurrection, making the weight implicit in وِزْر explicit through حِمْلًا.

terra: A known-answer question recalls that the heavens and earth were once joined and God split them apart; the divine opening of something compact into newly habitable space is a large-scale analogue of the section's concrete action.

luna: The source section names root ر غ ب and traces desire to breadth, then ends by turning desire toward the Lord. This ayah says the prophets called upon God “رَغَبًا وَرَهَبًا” and hurried to good; it makes that God-directed longing a prayerful stance. | terra: God recalls answering Zechariah's family prayer and says they called upon Him رَغَبًا وَرَهَبًا; desire directed into prayer supplies another form of the section's closing turn toward the Lord.
terra: God will fold the sky like a scroll, the exact physical reversal of the section's underlying movement from something folded and compact to something spread open.

luna: The source section defines root ص د ر as the bodily chest and says the image first shows a body being opened. This ayah locates the hearts within the breasts and contrasts them with eyes that may see while hearts are blind; it links the bodily chest to inward reception while marking a distinct kind of blindness. | terra: The ayah locates understanding hearts physically “in the breasts” and says those hearts can be blind; it both confirms the bodily container stressed by the section and limits bodily openness without perception.
terra: God says He placed no constriction in religion and then commands striving and holding fast, pairing freedom from حَرَج with fitness for a demanding charge as the section does.

luna: The source section cites a dictionary sense of ش ر ح as opening difficult words to reveal hidden meanings. This ayah says each challenge receives truth and “أَحْسَنَ تَفْسِيرًا,” a direct example of explanation bringing difficult speech into view.
terra: God says He gave Moses the Book and made Aaron a وَزِيرًا with him, showing the mission's weight answered by a supporting bearer alongside the prayer for inward capacity.
terra: Moses explicitly says he fears that Pharaoh's people will deny him; this supplies the named fear immediately before his breast constricts and his tongue fails to proceed in 26:13.

luna: The source section names root ص د ر for the bodily chest and contrasts opening with constriction. Musa says “يَضِيقُ صَدْرِي” and “لَا يَنطَلِقُ لِسَانِي”: tight chest and blocked speech directly counter the opened chest and speech made to flow. | terra: Moses says his breast constricts and his tongue does not proceed, joining the section's two bodily images: a tight chest and speech unable to open.
terra: God answers Moses' fear with a refusal of its conclusion and commands both brothers to go with the signs, completing the movement from constricted reluctance to divinely enabled mission.
terra: The revelation comes in a clear Arabic tongue, giving the positive speech state corresponding to a tongue released so that its hearers can understand.

luna: The source section names root ص د ر for the chest and describes opening as exposing what is inside. In this ayah “مَا تُكِنُّ صُدُورُهُمْ” is paired with what they disclose; the hidden and declared contents of breasts are both within God's knowledge.
terra: Moses recalls having killed one of Pharaoh's people and fears being killed, identifying the danger immediately before he asks for the more eloquent Aaron to support his speech.
terra: Moses identifies Aaron as more eloquent in tongue and asks that he be sent as support, explaining in another mission account the speech obstruction paired with his constricted breast.
terra: God answers the concern about Moses' tongue by promising to strengthen him through his brother and give both authority, another accepted form of making him fit for the charge.

luna: The source section names root ص د ر for the chest and describes opening as exposing what is inside. Here “مَا تُكِنُّ صُدُورُهُمْ” is paired with what they disclose as the surah closes on God's knowledge of their inner and outward state. | terra: God knows what people's breasts conceal and what they declare, another explicit boundary between the hidden interior and its outward manifestation.
terra: Those who tempt believers to follow them will carry their own burdens and others besides, again showing a load increased and shared in contrast to one removed.
terra: The arrival of the messengers again makes Lot distressed and straitened in capacity before they reassure him, a repeated mission scene of constriction answered by divine aid.
terra: During the siege, eyes swerve and hearts reach throats, making fear a bodily obstruction of breath and speech comparable to the section's chest as the felt site of constriction.
terra: Whatever mercy God opens for people cannot be withheld, making divine opening an act that creates access to a beneficial content rather than an empty expansion.

luna: The source section labels root و ز ر for a burden and gives it the image of a packed bundle. This ayah says no bearer “تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَىٰ” and pictures a laden person calling for help; it sets personal burden against the section's gift of having one's own load removed. | terra: No burdened soul bears another's burden, and even a heavily laden one calling for help has none of it carried; this vivid non-transfer fixes the personal force of “your burden” before its divine removal.

luna: The source section names root ص د ر for the chest and says opening brings an interior into view. This ayah calls Allah “عَلِيمٌ بِذَاتِ الصُّدُورِ” while speaking of the unseen, giving a concrete instance of what remains inside being known.

luna: The source section labels root و ز ر for the burden and gives it the image of a packed load. This ayah repeats “وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَىٰ” while saying God does not approve disbelief for His servants; it sets personal accountability beside the particular burden removed for the addressee. | terra: Amid the choice between ingratitude and gratitude, no burdened soul bears another's burden; inward orientation and personally borne consequence remain joined.

luna: The source section names root ش ر ح for an opened chest. Here Allah's opening is specifically “لِلْإِسْلَٰمِ” and leaves the person “عَلَىٰ نُورٍ مِّن رَّبِّهِۦ”; the result matches the section's point that what fills the opened space matters. | terra: The breast God has opened to Islam leaves its bearer upon light from his Lord, specifying what beneficially fills the space opened in the section.
terra: After the opened breast and light of 39:22, revelation makes skins shiver and then skins and hearts soften to God's remembrance; the body shows what receiving truth into that space does.
terra: On the approaching day, hearts are at throats while people choke back their anguish, another explicit bodily scene of inward pressure opposite to a breast given room.

luna: The source section says opening makes an interior visible and names root ص د ر for the chest. This ayah says God knows “مَا تُخْفِي الصُّدُورُ,” placing concealed contents in the chest before the One who sees them; it sharpens the section's hidden-inside detail. | terra: God knows what breasts conceal, directly corresponding to the hidden interior that the section's action of opening makes accessible.
terra: Those who dispute God's signs harbor only an unattainable greatness in their breasts, supplying a specific harmful content that shows why the direction and filling of inward space matter.

luna: The source section cites the dictionary sense of ش ر ح as opening difficult speech so its meanings appear. This ayah calls the Arabic Book one whose verses are detailed for people who know, a direct formulation of scriptural speech made explicit.
terra: People answer the invitation by claiming their hearts are under coverings and their ears bear a weight, a precise image of blocked reception opposite to an interior opened for truth.

luna: The source section names root ص د ر and says opening speech can make hidden meanings visible. This ayah joins God establishing truth by His words with His knowledge of “ذَاتِ الصُّدُورِ,” connecting revealed truth with what is held inside breasts.

terra: If God expanded provision without measure, people would transgress, so He sends it down in due measure; this is a specific nonlexical case where expansion itself can harm unless its content and measure are right.

terra: Pharaoh mocks Moses as one who can scarcely make himself clear; in the later confrontation this hostile claim tests, rather than erases, the prayer that his tongue be loosed and speech understood.
terra: فَإِنَّمَا يَسَّرْنَٰهُ بِلِسَانِكَ again makes the message easy by the Prophet's tongue, a direct nonlexical meeting of the section's ease and unknotted speech.
terra: The question whether hearts have their locks upon them supplies a precise barrier to reception, the opposite of making inward room for truth.
terra: إِنَّا فَتَحْنَا لَكَ gives the same divine “We,” completed opening, and beneficiary marked by لَكَ, while moving the opened object from the Prophet's breast to a manifest victory.
terra: The verse following “We opened for you” spells out its beneficiary sense through forgiveness, completion of favor, and guidance, clarifying what the section's emphatic لَكَ contributes.
terra: In the same opening-victory passage, God sends tranquility into believers' hearts so that faith increases, concretely naming a beneficial content placed within after divine opening.
terra: The Bedouins are told that faith has not yet entered their hearts, setting a boundary between verbal submission and the inward reception that the section's opened breast is meant to permit.

terra: A parchment spread open is a plausible physical analogue for the section's dictionary action of unfolding and spreading; the ayah does not itself connect that act to the breast or to explanation.

luna: The source section labels root و ز ر for the burden and gives it the image of a packed load. This ayah says “أَلَّا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَىٰ”; it makes the personal nature of a load explicit beside the section's remembered removal of the addressee's own burden. | terra: The scrolls of Moses and Abraham contain the maxim that no bearer bears another's burden, grounding the image of a personal load in an earlier revealed rule.
terra: God repeatedly says He made the Quran easy for remembrance, a broader scriptural instance of difficult divine speech being made accessible to receive and retain.
terra: After the account of ʿAd, the refrain again says God made the Quran easy for remembrance, confirming that the accessible-speech claim is deliberately repeated rather than incidental.
terra: After Thamud's destruction, the same declaration that the Quran was made easy for remembrance repeats the section's connection between divine speech and facilitated reception.
terra: After Lot's people, the repeated making-easy of the Quran supplies another distinct contextual occurrence of speech rendered accessible for remembrance.
terra: God teaches the human being clear expression, presenting intelligible speech as a divine enabling of the faculty whose knot Moses asks to have loosened.

terra: Believers are told to make room in gatherings and promised يَفْسَحِ ٱللَّهُ لَكُمْ; the social act of creating space and God's answering “for you” enact the section's spatial account of expansion.
